name: Behavioral analytics — live product analytics
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.one_line_definition: A product / growth / data team computes per-user and per-session live counters (sessions_today, events_in_window, time-to-Nth-event, last-active, page-velocity, funnel-step counters, retention features) and exposes them in <1 s to in-product personalization, lifecycle marketing triggers, CDP profiles, and live dashboards.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Power same-session in-app personalization: 'this user viewed 3 product pages and abandoned a cart in the last 5 minutes, surface a discount banner before they leave.' 2) Drive lifecycle / journey triggers ('user did event X N times in 24h, fire a Braze/Iterable campaign') with second-level freshness instead of warehouse-lag. 3) Feed a live product dashboard with sub-minute counters (concurrent sessions, signups in last 5 min, funnel-step conversion this hour) without waiting for Snowflake/BigQuery micro-batches. 4) Enrich a CDP profile (Segment, Hightouch, Adobe RTCDP, RudderStack) with rolling behavioral features (last_active_ts, session_count_7d, n_distinct_features_used_30d) that downstream tools read inline. 5) Compute retention / engagement aggregates (DAU/MAU, DAU/MAU stickiness, time-to-Nth-event, last-active recency) continuously rather than as nightly batch jobs.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Web/mobile/server-emitted behavioral events typically: page_view {ts, user_id, anonymous_id, session_id, url, referrer, device, country}, click / autocaptured_interaction {ts, user_id, element, page}, custom_event {ts, user_id, event_name, props{}}, session_start / session_end {ts, user_id, session_id, duration_ms}, signup {ts, user_id, plan, source}, feature_adopted {ts, user_id, feature_name}, purchase / conversion {ts, user_id, sku, amount}, identify {ts, anonymous_id -> user_id, traits{}}. Volume is dominated by page_view and autocaptured click events. Key dimensions: user_id, anonymous_id, session_id, account_id (B2B), feature_name, event_name, funnel_step, page/route, cohort_id.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of count, n_unique, velocity, recency, and distribution primitives in tumbling and sliding windows. Per-user: count(events, 1m/5m/1h/24h), n_unique(page_url, session), velocity(events / minute), recency(last_event_ts), time_since_signup, time_to_first_purchase, time_to_Nth_event (Aha-moment), funnel_step_reached (max-seen), distribution(event_name over 24h). Per-session: count(events), n_unique(pages), session_duration, scroll_depth_max, last_event_ts. Per-account (B2B): n_unique(active_users, 7d), n_unique(features_used, 30d). Per-cohort / global: count(active_sessions_now), count(signups_5m), funnel-step conversion ratios. DAU/MAU is really n_unique(user_id) over tumbling 1d/30d windows — exact at low cardinality, HLL at scale.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite. Primary keys are user_id (authenticated), anonymous_id (pre-auth), session_id, account_id / workspace_id (B2B), plus secondary keys feature_name, funnel_name, page_route, cohort_id. The (user_id, feature_name) and (user_id, funnel_step) pairs are common.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: All three: sliding for 'events_in_last_N_minutes' personalization signals, tumbling for hourly/daily counters fed to dashboards and warehouses, session windows (inactivity timeout, typically 30 min on web / 5 min on mobile) for sessionization itself. Approximate aggregates are perfectly acceptable: HLL for DAU/MAU and unique-page-views, CMS / Top-K for 'most-viewed pages right now', t-digest for session-duration percentiles. Exact counts are required only where the number drives a contract (billing pages viewed) or a regulatory disclosure.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once is acceptable for the vast majority of behavioral analytics — a slightly over-counted page_view does not break a dashboard or a personalization decision. Idempotency by (event_id, user_id) is industry standard at the SDK layer (Segment, Snowplow, RudderStack all dedupe on event_id), and is nice-to-have but not load-bearing in beava. Strict exactly-once is only required if the counter feeds usage-based billing — that belongs in use case 14b, not here.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <50 ms is the operational target for in-app personalization gates ('decide whether to show the discount banner before the page paints'); <200 ms is the widely-cited industry latency budget for real-time personalization (InfoWorld, Algolia, Databricks all converge on ~100–200 ms end-to-end). Live dashboards tolerate 1–2 s. beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits well inside both budgets.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to a few seconds end-to-end is the differentiating goal vs. the warehouse stack. The published numbers from incumbents bound the competitive gap: Mixpanel ingests 99% of events under 1 minute (mobile SDKs add a 1–2 min buffering delay); Amplitude charts show new events in seconds-to-minutes with a streaming-export p95 latency target of 60 s; Adobe RTCDP streaming segmentation can take up to 5 minutes to qualify a profile and 15+ minutes through the CDP layer for non-edge data; Snowflake Dynamic Tables have a 1-minute minimum target lag for streaming reverse ETL; warehouse-resident counters via dbt typically refresh at 5–60 minute cadence. beava's push-on-event, no-broker model targets sub-second, which is the freshness gap the README claims.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for a typical buyer is in the 1k–50k/s range; large product-analytics tenants are higher. Public reference: Amplitude processes ~5 trillion events processed lifetime (Firebolt blog) with sustained ingest rates that imply millions of EPS aggregate across their fleet; a single Mixpanel-class mid-market tenant typically lands at 1k–20k EPS. Adobe RTCDP's streaming segmentation explicitly caps at 1,500 EPS inbound per tenant. A single beava node at ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) comfortably covers a single mid-to-large product-analytics customer; very large multi-tenant SaaS analytics vendors would still need horizontal partitioning (which beava v0 does not provide in-process). [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Strongly read-heavy at the personalization / dashboard tier (each user-facing impression reads 5–50 features for one occasional write), more balanced at the event-ingestion tier (every event is a write, plus periodic reads when a journey-engine or dashboard polls). Net across the deployment, behavioral analytics is the most read-heavy of the README-stated domains — the README's own framing of this use case as 'read-heavy' is accurate.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by user_id and anonymous_id cardinality. A typical mid-market product-analytics buyer has 100k–10M MAU and 10x that in anonymous_ids per year. At ~200–500 B per per-entity rolling-feature vector (a handful of counters + HLLs + recency timestamps), 10M active entities is ~2–5 GB; 100M is ~20–50 GB. Add session-level state (~50–200 B per active session, evicted on session-end) and per-account / per-cohort aggregates and a typical buyer lands at single-digit-to-low-tens of GB hot state — fits in RAM on a single modern box. The pathological case is unauthenticated traffic (anonymous_id explosion) which mandates aggressive TTL eviction; beava's refuse-on-network-FS and in-memory-only model fits this if TTL/eviction is wired up correctly. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly-growing on user_id (bounded by product reach). Explosive on anonymous_id (every untracked browser, multiplied by cookie churn). Bounded on event_name (tens to low hundreds typically), feature_name, funnel_step, route. Explosive on session_id but with built-in TTL via session-window inactivity. Slowly-growing on account_id (B2B).
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds-to-minutes for hot session features. 1–24 hours for in-session and lifecycle-trigger features (e.g., 'events in last 24h'). 7–30 days for retention features (DAU/MAU, stickiness, last-active). 90–365 days for cohort-level behavioral history. Beyond 30 days the analytics use case typically swaps to the warehouse — beava is the hot tier, not the archive.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 5–30 features per personalization decision (vs. 20–100+ for fraud) — fewer because product decisions are usually simpler ('show banner if abandoned_cart_5m=true AND session_count_7d>2') and the heavy lift is event collection, not feature breadth. Lifecycle-marketing triggers typically read 3–15 features. Dashboards batch-read 50–500 features at once but tolerate higher latency.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe. Behavioral analytics is derived state, not money or regulated record. Losing 5 minutes of session counters during a node restart degrades a dashboard and a few personalization decisions but does not produce a financial, regulatory, or auditable error. beava's WAL + snapshot story is more than sufficient; in fact many buyers in this space (Mixpanel, Amplitude, PostHog) explicitly publish multi-day SLA windows for batch pipelines because best-effort is the norm. The exception is when the counter is also feeding usage-based billing (see use case 14b) or is the source-of-truth for an audited engagement metric (rare).
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for single-binary regional, sidecar-next-to-event-collector, and per-tenant-in-SaaS topologies. A product analytics vendor (Mixpanel/Amplitude/PostHog-class) could embed beava as the per-tenant 'hot tier' behind their ingestion API; an in-house team could run beava as a single sidecar next to their SDK collector. Multi-region active-active is rarely required because behavioral analytics is usually region-affinity-tolerant (a user's session is pinned to one region). The hard limit is that beava v0 has no in-process sharding, so a single very large tenant (>684k EPS or >50 GB hot state) must hand-shard externally.

commercial_fit.who_buys: (a) Product / growth / data engineering teams at SaaS, e-commerce, fintech, media, gaming buying or replacing Mixpanel / Amplitude / PostHog / Heap / Pendo / June. (b) Marketing/CRM engineering teams behind a CDP (Segment, RudderStack, Hightouch, Adobe RTCDP, Treasure Data) wanting fresher computed attributes than reverse-ETL can deliver. (c) Lifecycle marketing engineering at Braze/Iterable customers who need real-time event counts to fire 'did X N times in 24h' canvases. (d) ML/personalization platform teams running same-session personalization (Algolia, RudderStack engine, in-house). The buyer in this domain is product / growth / platform — explicitly NOT the risk / fraud team.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Product analytics market is sized at $10.6–14.8B in 2025 by various analysts, growing at 12–23% CAGR to $30–41B by 2030–2034 (Research and Markets, Fortune Business Insights, The Business Research Co., Polaris). Mixpanel, Amplitude (NASDAQ:AMPL), PostHog, Heap (Contentsquare), Pendo, Glassbox, FullStory together represent the public-comparable revenue. Pricing reference: PostHog free up to 1M events/mo then $0.00031/event; Mixpanel ~$0.00028/event after the 1M free tier, putting a 10M-event/mo tenant at $2.5k/mo and a 1B-event/mo tenant at $250k+/mo. The CDP adjacency (Segment, Adobe RTCDP, Treasure Data, RudderStack, Hightouch) is a multi-billion-dollar market in its own right. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) Same-session personalization is the named industry trend for 2025–2026 (Algolia, Hightouch, Contentful, Bloomreach all publishing on it) — the buyer can no longer accept warehouse-lag for in-product decisions. 2) AI-driven personalization engines (contextual bandits, LLM-driven copy) need rolling behavioral features at the moment-of-decision, not minutes later. 3) Mixpanel/Amplitude/PostHog pricing-per-event pressure is pushing larger buyers to build hybrid stacks where the hot tier is self-hosted and the warehouse is the cold archive — the textbook seam for beava. 4) CDP-to-marketing-tool reverse-ETL lag (often 5–60 min) is the published gap that 'streaming reverse ETL' products (Hightouch Streaming, Census event-streaming) are explicitly trying to close. 5) GDPR / CCPA pressure pushes buyers toward short TTLs and in-region processing, which favors a single-binary in-region hot tier over a global SaaS analytics provider.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: GDPR (consent + right-to-erasure on user_id and anonymous_id; TTL-by-default and tombstone on delete are required), CCPA / CPRA (same shape, plus Do-Not-Sell), Apple ATT / Google Privacy Sandbox (anonymous_id half-life is shrinking, which raises pressure on first-party real-time analytics). SOC 2 is table-stakes for any vendor selling to enterprise. Not regulator-grade durability (this is not AML), but PII handling matters — beava's lack of TLS/auth in v0 is a real blocker for any production deployment outside a trusted VPC.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 1–3 days to a working 'session counters + last-active + page-velocity' demo on a laptop using beava's @bv.event + @bv.table primitives, against a Segment or PostHog event source. 1–2 weeks to a production pilot in front of a same-session personalization or lifecycle-trigger workflow, gated mostly by adding TLS/auth (the v0 gaps below) and wiring up TTL/eviction policy for the anonymous_id cardinality.

competition.incumbents: Generic real-time stack the buyer might assemble: Redis (counters + HLL + sorted-sets + Lua) is the overwhelming default for hot per-user counters; ClickHouse / Pinot / Druid / Tinybird for live dashboards on event streams; Kafka + Flink (or Spark Real-Time Mode, Materialize, RisingWave) for stream-processed counters; Tecton / Hopsworks / Chalk / Fennel as managed online feature stores for personalization features; Snowflake Dynamic Tables / BigQuery streaming + dbt for warehouse-resident counters with 1–60 min lag.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Product analytics SaaS: Mixpanel, Amplitude, PostHog, Heap (Contentsquare), Pendo, June, Glassbox, FullStory, Microsoft Clarity, Datadog Product Analytics. Event-collection layer / behavioral CDP: Segment (Twilio), RudderStack, Snowplow, Tealium, mParticle, Adobe RTCDP, Treasure Data, Bloomreach Engagement. Lifecycle / engagement: Braze, Iterable, Customer.io, OneSignal. Same-session personalization: Algolia, Hightouch (Streaming), Sitecore Personalize, Dynamic Yield. None of these is a pure feature-server — they bundle ingestion, schema, storage, querying, dashboards, and activation. beava would naturally sit underneath one of these (powering the hot per-user counter tier) rather than replace any of them outright.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Sub-second feature freshness vs. the incumbents' published 1–60 min lag (Mixpanel ingest ~1 min, Amplitude charts seconds-to-minutes, Adobe RTCDP streaming-segmentation up to 5 min, dbt-on-warehouse 5–60 min) — this is the explicit 'freshness gap' beava's README leans on. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives cover the count / n_unique / velocity / recency / distribution / distance features this domain literally lives on, without writing Lua-on-Redis or Flink SQL. 3) Single binary, no Kafka / Flink / Spark / Redis-cluster — fits a sidecar-next-to-collector or per-tenant-hot-tier embedding model. 4) Apache-2.0, no open-core — attractive to vendors (Segment / RudderStack / PostHog-class) who might embed it inside their stack without dragging in a competitor's managed cloud. 5) Push-on-event over HTTP/JSON :8080 or framed TCP+msgpack :8081 maps directly to how Segment, RudderStack, and in-house SDKs already produce events. 6) Recency / 'last-active' and distance / 'page-velocity' primitives are first-class, which on Redis are hand-rolled and on warehouses are simply too slow.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth in v0 — disqualifying for any production SaaS deployment that handles user PII (which is most of them); restricts beava today to in-VPC / behind-mTLS-proxy. 2) No in-process sharding — a single very large tenant (>684k EPS or tens of GB hot state) has to hand-shard externally. 3) No SQL / ad-hoc-query surface — incumbents like Mixpanel, Amplitude, and ClickHouse let analysts cut new funnels and cohorts on the fly; beava only serves the features it has been told to compute. This is a fundamental product gap for the 'replace my product-analytics tool' framing and forces beava into the 'hot feature tier behind the analytics tool' role. 4) No event archive / replay / backfill — losing 5 minutes of session state on restart is fine, but the buyer still needs Parquet/lakehouse downstream for retroactive analysis (Heap-style retroactive event definition is not on the table). 5) No triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — lifecycle marketing is exactly the use case that wants this (use case 17 calls it out). 6) No multi-tenancy primitives (namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate limits) for a SaaS vendor wanting to embed beava across thousands of customers. 7) No native consent / GDPR-delete primitive (tombstone-by-user_id) — must be implemented on top.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: web SDKs (Segment analytics.js, RudderStack JS, Snowplow, PostHog JS, Mixpanel JS), mobile SDKs (Segment, Amplitude, Mixpanel, Braze, PostHog), server SDKs and webhooks, Kafka / Kinesis (for buyers already on a streaming bus), Snowplow collector. beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 fits the SDK / webhook producer path with no shim; the TCP+msgpack :8081 path fits the higher-throughput collector deployments. Consumers: in-app personalization gates (Algolia, Hightouch Streaming, in-house), lifecycle marketing engines (Braze action-based delivery, Iterable Journeys, Customer.io), dashboards (Grafana, custom React/SSE, Tinybird), CDP profile-enrichment hooks (Segment Functions, RudderStack Transformations, Adobe RTCDP edge), ML scorers (XGBoost / contextual bandits) reading per-user features via batch_get.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Mostly an external rules engine on the lifecycle / journey side (Braze canvases, Iterable workflows, Customer.io flows) and an ML scorer on the personalization side (contextual bandits, ranking models, LLM-driven copy). beava remains the pure feature backend in both cases; it does not become the scoring engine itself.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public users of beava on this use case identified. [uncertain] Comparable production references at incumbents: Amplitude publicly cites ~5 trillion events processed lifetime; Mixpanel publishes its 'under-1-minute ingestion for 99% of events' SLA; Adobe RTCDP publishes its streaming-segmentation cap (1,500 EPS, up-to-5-min qualification); MakeMyTrip on Databricks publishes a 'millisecond personalization at scale' case study; Hightouch Streaming Reverse ETL publishes named customer wins for same-session personalization; PostHog publishes per-tenant event volume in their pricing analysis pages. Snowplow + Databricks + Redis combinations are widely deployed for the same shape of workload.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads located on this topic. [uncertain] Broader community signal is strong: Hightouch's 'same-session personalization' announcement and follow-up content (2024–2025), InfoWorld 'The 200ms latency: a developer's guide to real-time personalization' (2025), Algolia real-time personalization eBook, Databricks Real-Time Mode blog (2025), Hacker News threads on PostHog self-hosting and Mixpanel pricing, Reddit r/dataengineering threads on warehouse-counter freshness vs. Redis hot-tier hybrids.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated behavioral-analytics / live-product-analytics demo identified in the repository. The closest existing artifact is /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ecommerce (events.jsonl + schema.json with PageView / AddToCart / Purchase event shapes) which is adjacent and reusable but is framed as e-commerce/recsys-style rather than as a generic product-analytics 'session counters + funnels + retention' demo. A purpose-built demo (sessions_today, events_in_5m, time_to_first_purchase, last_active, funnel_step_reached) would be a natural addition. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Low / passive. This is a passive-load domain — there is no active adversary trying to evade the analytics counter. The drift is from product changes (new events, schema evolution, new funnels) and from privacy mechanics (cookie / anonymous_id churn, consent revocation), not from an attacker. This dramatically simplifies the operational story compared to fraud (use cases 1a–4) — the buyer is allergic to outages but tolerant of slightly approximate counts.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Replacing a product-analytics tool's analyst surface (ad-hoc funnels, cohorts, paths, retroactive event definition, session replay) — beava only serves features it has been told to compute, so it sits underneath Mixpanel/Amplitude/PostHog, not in place of them. 2) Long historical lookback (>30–90 d) — beava is in-memory only; the warehouse remains the cold archive. 3) Heap-style retroactive analysis (defining a new event after the fact and re-running history) — not possible without an event archive. 4) Cross-entity SQL joins across user × event × cohort × account — that is OLAP territory (ClickHouse, Pinot, Druid, Snowflake, BigQuery), not feature-server territory. 5) Acting as the consent / privacy registry — beava can receive a 'delete this user_id' command but is not the system of record for consent. 6) Source-of-truth for usage-based billing — that belongs in use case 14b with stricter exactly-once and durability requirements.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination and an auth model (token / mTLS) on :8081 and :8090 — without these, beava cannot handle user PII outside a strictly trusted VPC, which rules out any SaaS deployment. 2) Per-entity TTL / sliding-window eviction with a documented memory budget — anonymous_id cardinality is the dominant operational risk and the buyer needs a 'set max RAM, evict-by-TTL-then-LRU' guarantee. 3) HLL / Bloom / CMS / Top-K / t-digest as documented first-class aggregations to keep DAU/MAU and unique-page-views tractable at high cardinality. 4) A GDPR-style 'tombstone-by-user_id' primitive that cascades across all per-(user_id, *) features atomically, with a documented latency bound. 5) Triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — necessary for lifecycle-marketing use cases (did X N times in Y window) without polling. 6) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting for vendors embedding beava across many customer workspaces. 7) Schema evolution: behavioral events change weekly; the @bv.event story needs to tolerate adding a new field without dropping state. 8) An optional event-archive sink (S3 / Parquet / Iceberg) so the cold tier can live alongside without forcing the buyer to dual-write. 9) In-process or sidecar sharding by key prefix for tenants that exceed a single box. 10) A documented identity-stitch story (anonymous_id -> user_id on identify) so per-user features can survive sign-up.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes for the lifecycle-marketing / journey-engine slice ('user did X N times in 24h → fire campaign'); polling 5–30 features per user per minute to threshold them is wasteful, and the buyer in this slice is exactly the one cited in use case 17. Pure live-dashboard and same-session-personalization slices need only feature serving (the read is happening anyway because something is about to render), not triggers.
